items.title: An Open Seat at the Fed: Why Atlanta Fed President Bostic's Retirement Matters
items.body:
When a regional Federal Reserve Bank president steps down, the news rarely makes the front page. Yet the retirement of Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic puts a spotlight on one of the least understood parts of U.S. monetary policy: who picks the people who help set interest rates, and why that process matters to markets.

*This article is for general information only and is not investment advice.*

## What Bostic's Departure Means

Raphael Bostic announced he would retire from the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta after nearly two decades in public service and a tenure that began in 2017. He was the first Black president in the history of the Federal Reserve System. His exit leaves the Atlanta Fed's top job to be filled through a process that is quite different from how the Fed's Washington-based leaders are chosen.

The Atlanta Fed covers Alabama, Florida, Georgia, and parts of Louisiana, Mississippi, and Tennessee. That makes it a valuable window into a fast-growing part of the country, with data on housing, labor markets, and business conditions that feed directly into the central bank's thinking.

## How the Fed Is Organized

The Federal Reserve System has two main layers:

- **The Board of Governors** in Washington, D.C., has seven members. Each is nominated by the President of the United States and confirmed by the Senate to a 14-year term, staggered so that one seat comes open every two years.
- **Twelve regional Reserve Banks**, including Atlanta, Boston, Chicago, and San Francisco, each led by a president.

Monetary policy decisions come from the **Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC)**. It has twelve voting members: the seven governors, the president of the New York Fed, and four of the other eleven regional presidents, who vote on a rotating annual basis. All twelve regional presidents attend meetings and take part in the discussion, but only those holding a vote at that time cast ballots on the interest-rate decision.

## How Regional Presidents Are Chosen

This is the key difference between governors and regional presidents.

1. **A local board of directors leads the search.** Each Reserve Bank has a board of nine directors. Three of them (known as Class C directors) are appointed by the Board of Governors; six are chosen locally, with a mix of bankers and members of the public representing business, labor, and community interests.
2. **The directors nominate a candidate.** The non-banker directors play the leading role in selecting a president.
3. **The Board of Governors in Washington must approve.** The appointment is not final until the Board of Governors signs off. Regional presidents are not nominated by the White House and do not require Senate confirmation.
4. **Terms are set by the bank, not by statute.** Presidents are appointed for five-year terms, and the system has rules about retirement ages for them.

The design was intentional. Congress created the system in 1913 to blend national oversight with regional input, so that decisions would not reflect only the views of Washington or Wall Street.

## Governors vs. Regional Presidents

| | Board governors | Regional bank presidents |
|---|---|---|
| Selected by | President, confirmed by the Senate | Local board, approved by the Board of Governors |
| Term | 14 years | 5 years |
| FOMC vote | Always | Only in certain years (New York always) |
| Political process | Public, high-profile | Mostly internal |

Because regional presidents come through a different route, they often bring different backgrounds: academic economists, former bank supervisors, or people with deep business roots. They also have their own research staffs, which can produce independent economic analysis that sometimes diverges from the Washington consensus.

## Why Succession Becomes a Market Story

Investors pay attention to the Fed because its choices on interest rates influence mortgages, corporate borrowing costs, stock valuations, and the value of the dollar. A change in who sits around the FOMC table can matter in several ways:

- **Voting balance.** Each regional president who votes is one of twelve voices. Analysts often sort officials into "hawks" (more focused on controlling inflation) and "doves" (more focused on employment). A new president could lean differently from the predecessor, although a single vote rarely decides an outcome.
- **Signals about direction.** Public speeches and written commentary from Fed officials are closely read for hints on future policy. A new president's first remarks are watched for clues about their thinking.
- **Political attention.** In recent years, the White House has shown unusually strong interest in the direction of the central bank, from public comments about rates to debates over appointments to the Board of Governors. Because the governors' side of the process involves the President directly, attention has naturally extended to the regional side as well, even though the Board of Governors' approval is the only federal role in picking a regional president.
- **Independence questions.** The Fed is designed to make decisions based on economic data rather than short-term political pressure. Any vacancy invites questions about how well that structure holds up, which is one reason the selection process draws more scrutiny than it once did.

## What to Watch Next

- **Timing.** Searches for a regional president often take months. An interim leader, usually a first vice president, typically steps in while the search runs.
- **The candidate's profile.** Whether the board picks an academic, a veteran Fed staffer, or an outsider from business can hint at the bank's priorities.
- **Approval by the Board of Governors.** This step is usually routine, but it is the one place where Washington has a formal say.
- **The next FOMC meetings.** Look at how the committee's statements, projections, and any dissents evolve as personnel change.

## The Bottom Line

Raphael Bostic's retirement is more than a personnel notice. It is a reminder that the Fed is a layered institution, and that the people who shape U.S. interest-rate policy arrive by several distinct paths. Understanding how regional presidents are chosen, and how they differ from governors, helps explain why a leadership change in Atlanta can attract attention from Washington to Wall Street, even if the immediate effect on rates is limited.

*Information in this article reflects publicly available descriptions of the Federal Reserve's structure. Details of the succession process and its timing may change, so check official Federal Reserve sources for the latest updates.*

items.title: Open Enrollment Season: How to Compare ACA Marketplace and Medicare Plans Before the Deadlines
items.body:
Every fall, millions of Americans face the same set of choices: keep the health plan they have, or switch. Medicare's annual enrollment period for most people runs from Oct. 15 to Dec. 7, and most Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace deadlines fall in December or January. With the clock running, a short list of questions can help you compare plans in a clear, orderly way.

*This article is general information, not personal insurance, tax or legal advice. Rules, prices and deadlines vary by state and by plan, so confirm details with official sources before you decide.*

## Know Which Calendar Applies to You

Start by identifying which system you belong to, because the dates differ.

- **Medicare (Oct. 15 – Dec. 7):** During this window, people already in Medicare can switch between Original Medicare and a Medicare Advantage plan, change Advantage plans, or join, switch or drop a Part D prescription drug plan. Changes generally take effect Jan. 1.
- **Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment (Jan. 1 – March 31):** People already in a Medicare Advantage plan can make one change during this period, such as switching to another Advantage plan or returning to Original Medicare. It is not a second chance for everyone, so check whether it applies to you.
- **ACA marketplace (varies by state):** On HealthCare.gov, the standard pattern has been to enroll by Dec. 15 for coverage starting Jan. 1, with open enrollment continuing into mid-January for coverage that starts later. Some state-run marketplaces set their own dates, and a few extend them. Check your state's exchange for its exact schedule.
- **Employer plans:** If you get coverage at work, your company sets its own enrollment window, often in the fall. This guide focuses on Medicare and marketplace plans.

If you are turning 65 or are newly eligible, your Initial Enrollment Period works differently from the annual window. Missing it can lead to late-enrollment penalties for some parts of Medicare, so look up your personal dates.

## Question 1: What Will This Plan Really Cost Me?

The monthly premium is the number people notice first, but it is only one piece of the cost.

- **Premium:** The fixed monthly amount. For marketplace plans, this is the figure *after* any premium tax credit. Enter accurate income and household information on the application, since the credit depends on your expected income for the coming year.
- **Deductible:** What you pay before the plan starts sharing costs for many services.
- **Copays and coinsurance:** Flat fees or percentages you pay for visits, tests, procedures and prescriptions.
- **Out-of-pocket maximum:** The most you could pay in a year for covered, in-network care. After that, the plan pays covered costs.

A plan with a low premium may carry a high deductible. A plan with a higher premium may cost less overall if you expect regular care. A useful exercise is to estimate your likely year: how many doctor visits, specialist appointments, prescriptions and possible procedures you expect, and then add up what each plan would charge.

### A Note on Marketplace Subsidies

The size of premium tax credits is set by federal law and has changed in recent years. Do not assume last year's price will repeat. Compare your actual 2027 quote, using the official marketplace's window-shopping tools or the Plan Finder, rather than relying on past experience. Households that qualify for cost-sharing reductions should look closely at Silver-level plans, which can lower deductibles and copays for eligible enrollees.

## Question 2: Are My Doctors and Hospitals In the Network?

Networks are one of the most common reasons people regret a plan choice.

- **Look up each doctor, specialist and hospital you use** in the plan's own provider directory, and confirm by phone with the office. Directories can be out of date.
- **Understand the plan type.** HMO plans usually require you to use in-network providers and may require referrals. PPO plans generally offer more flexibility at higher cost. EPO plans typically do not cover out-of-network care except in emergencies.
- **Original Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage:** Original Medicare is accepted by most doctors and hospitals nationwide that take Medicare. Medicare Advantage plans use networks and often include extras, but they may restrict you to a local area and may require prior authorization for some services.
- **Check where you travel or live part of the year.** If you spend months away, confirm what the plan covers outside its home area.

## Question 3: Does It Cover My Prescription Drugs?

Drug coverage can change from year to year, even when you stay with the same plan.

- **Check the formulary** (the plan's list of covered drugs) for every medication you take, including the dose and form.
- **Look at the tier** each drug falls into, since higher tiers cost more.
- **Ask about restrictions** such as prior authorization, step therapy (trying a cheaper drug first) and quantity limits.
- **Confirm your pharmacy.** Some plans offer lower prices at preferred pharmacies.
- **Read your Annual Notice of Change.** Medicare plans send this document in the fall. It explains changes to costs, coverage and networks for next year, and it is easy to overlook.

For Medicare Part D, an annual out-of-pocket cap on covered drug spending now exists, thanks to changes made by the Inflation Reduction Act. The cap was $2,000 in 2025 and is adjusted for inflation in later years. Check the Medicare Plan Finder for the exact 2027 figure. Many plans also offer the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, which lets you spread out-of-pocket drug costs across the year in monthly installments instead of paying all at once. Spreading the cost does not lower the total.

## Question 4: What Is the Worst-Case Scenario?

Out-of-pocket caps are what protect you from a very expensive illness or accident.

- **ACA marketplace plans** have a federal annual limit on out-of-pocket spending for in-network, covered essential health benefits. The limit is adjusted each year and is substantial for an individual, so look up the figure for the plan year you are choosing.
- **Medicare Advantage plans** must include an annual limit on in-network out-of-pocket costs for Part A and Part B services. Limits differ by plan.
- **Original Medicare** has no annual out-of-pocket cap for Parts A and B. Many people add a Medigap (Medicare Supplement) policy or have other coverage, such as retiree or employer benefits, to help fill that gap. Medigap policies are sold separately, and your best time to buy one without medical underwriting is usually during your Medigap open enrollment period, so check the rules in your state.

If you are weighing Original Medicare with Medigap against Medicare Advantage, think about predictability versus flexibility. Medigap typically means higher monthly premiums but fewer surprises and wide provider choice. Advantage plans often have lower premiums and extra benefits but come with network rules and cost-sharing that varies by service.

## Question 5: What Extra Benefits Do I Actually Use?

Plans, particularly Medicare Advantage plans, advertise dental, vision, hearing, gym memberships and over-the-counter allowances. These can be valuable, but only if you use them.

- Check the dollar limits and what is covered.
- Look at whether your own dentist or eye doctor participates.
- Compare the value of these extras to any difference in premiums or cost-sharing.

## A Practical Step-by-Step Checklist

1. **Mark your deadlines** on a calendar today, including the date by which you need to act for coverage to begin Jan. 1.
2. **Gather your information:** a list of doctors, medications with doses, preferred pharmacy, expected income (for marketplace subsidies) and your current plan documents.
3. **Read your current plan's notice of changes** before assuming it will stay the same.
4. **Use official comparison tools:** Medicare.gov's Plan Finder for Medicare, and HealthCare.gov or your state exchange for marketplace plans.
5. **Compare total expected cost,** not just premium: premium plus likely out-of-pocket spending, with the out-of-pocket maximum as your worst case.
6. **Verify networks and formularies by phone,** not only online.
7. **Get free, unbiased help.** State Health Insurance Assistance Programs (SHIPs) offer free counseling on Medicare. Marketplace navigators and certified application counselors can help with ACA enrollment at no charge.
8. **Save confirmation** of your enrollment and watch for your first bill and insurance cards.

## Beware of Common Pitfalls

- **Aggressive marketing.** Be cautious about unsolicited calls, mailers and ads. Legitimate Medicare plans cannot generally call you unprompted to sell a plan, and you should never share your Medicare number with someone you do not trust.
- **Assuming auto-renewal is automatic savings.** Staying put is convenient, but premiums, networks and drug lists change. A quick review can reveal a better fit or catch a cost increase.
- **Reporting inaccurate income.** For marketplace plans, a big difference between estimated and actual income can result in repaying part of your credit at tax time.
- **Waiting until the last day.** Websites get busy near deadlines, and a missed window may leave you without coverage options until the next open enrollment unless you qualify for a special enrollment period due to a life event.

## The Bottom Line

Open enrollment is a limited-time chance to make sure your coverage matches your health needs and your budget. You do not need to be an insurance expert to do it well. Focus on five things: what you will really pay, whether your doctors are in the network, whether your drugs are covered, how much you could pay in a bad year, and which extras you will use. Then confirm the facts with official sources and a free counselor, and make your decision before the deadline arrives.

*Deadlines, benefit amounts and subsidy rules change. Verify current details at Medicare.gov, HealthCare.gov or your state marketplace, and consult a licensed professional for advice about your situation.*

items.title: Picks and Shovels Wobble: Why AI Infrastructure Stocks Like Vertiv and Quanta Fell Sharply
items.body:
When investors talk about the artificial intelligence boom, the spotlight usually lands on chip designers and the companies building large language models. But a quieter group of businesses sits underneath all of it: the firms that supply the electrical gear, cooling systems and construction labor that make AI data centers run. In early November, shares of several of these "picks and shovels" companies, including Vertiv and Quanta Services, fell sharply, with some moves reaching double digits over a short stretch. This article explains what these companies do, why their stocks had climbed so far, and what the sudden swing may say about expectations for AI spending.

*This article is for general information only. It is not investment advice, and it does not recommend buying or selling any security.*

## What "picks and shovels" means here

The phrase comes from the California Gold Rush. The story goes that the people who reliably made money were not always the prospectors, but the merchants who sold them tools. In the AI boom, the same idea is applied to companies that profit from the build-out of computing capacity no matter which AI model or application ultimately wins.

An AI data center is not just a warehouse full of servers. It needs:

- **Power delivery:** transformers, switchgear, backup generators, batteries and power distribution units that bring large amounts of electricity safely to racks of processors.
- **Cooling:** AI chips generate far more heat than traditional servers, pushing operators toward liquid cooling and advanced thermal management.
- **Electrical construction:** crews that build substations, run high-voltage lines and connect new facilities to the grid.

## Who the companies are

**Vertiv** designs and sells critical digital infrastructure, including power management and thermal systems for data centers. As rack power densities rise with AI hardware, demand for its cooling and power products has grown.

**Quanta Services** is a specialty contractor focused on electric transmission, distribution and other energy infrastructure. Its crews build and upgrade the power lines and substations that data centers depend on, which links its fortunes to both utility spending and data center growth.

Other companies in the same broad category include makers of electrical equipment, generators and turbines, as well as engineering and construction firms. They differ widely in business mix, so a move in one name does not always mean the same thing for another.

## Why these stocks had run so far

Several forces helped lift this group over the past couple of years:

1. **Surging capital spending plans.** Large cloud providers and AI developers have announced very large multiyear investment plans for data centers. Suppliers of physical equipment can point to order backlogs that reflect those plans.
2. **Power as a bottleneck.** Many analysts have argued that access to electricity, not just access to chips, limits how fast new capacity can come online. Anything that eases or serves that bottleneck drew investor attention.
3. **Long lead times and pricing power.** Equipment such as large transformers can take a long time to manufacture, which supports pricing and visibility into future revenue.
4. **A simpler story than picking an AI winner.** Investors who were unsure which AI model or software company would prevail found it appealing to own the suppliers that benefit from the build-out in general.

When a group of stocks rises quickly on a clear narrative, expectations tend to rise with it. Valuations can come to assume that growth continues at a strong pace for years.

## Why a sharp drop can happen

A double-digit decline in a short period usually reflects a shift in sentiment more than a sudden change in a company's day-to-day operations. Several factors commonly contribute to moves like this:

- **High expectations leave little room for error.** If a stock already prices in strong growth, even a modest disappointment or a cautious comment can trigger large selling.
- **Doubts about the durability of AI spending.** Any sign that customers might slow, delay or reshape their data center plans, or questions about whether AI investment will earn adequate returns, can ripple through every company tied to that spending.
- **Crowded positioning.** When many investors hold the same winning trade, a few sellers can push prices down quickly as others rush to reduce exposure.
- **Broader market and rate moves.** Shifts in interest rate expectations or a general pullback in growth and technology shares can hit richly valued stocks harder.
- **Company-specific news.** Earnings reports, guidance changes and order updates can move individual names in ways that then spill over to similar companies.

It is worth noting that the exact size of each move depends on the stock and the dates measured, and that prices change daily. Readers should check current market data from a reliable source for up-to-date figures.

## What the swing says about AI spending expectations

The pullback does not by itself show that AI investment is ending. Rather, it highlights how much of the market's optimism rests on the assumption that spending will stay high and keep growing. A few takeaways stand out:

- **Suppliers are a leveraged read on customers' budgets.** Their revenue depends on the spending decisions of a small number of very large buyers. If those budgets look uncertain, supplier shares can react strongly.
- **The "safe" label has limits.** Picks-and-shovels companies may be less exposed to any single AI product failing, but they are not immune to a slowdown in the overall build-out or to a reset in valuations.
- **Timing matters.** Orders, backlogs and revenue can lag announcements. Investors may be weighing how quickly announced projects turn into actual deliveries and sales.
- **Physical constraints cut both ways.** Limits on power, equipment and skilled labor can support demand, but they can also delay projects and push out when revenue is recognized.

## What to watch next

For readers following the sector, a few indicators may help put future swings in context:

- Capital spending guidance from major cloud and AI companies in their quarterly reports.
- Order backlogs, book-to-bill ratios and management commentary from equipment and construction suppliers.
- Utility plans for grid upgrades and new generation tied to data center demand.
- Signals on power availability, permitting and equipment lead times.
- Broader market conditions, including interest rate expectations.

## The bottom line

The recent drop in shares of Vertiv, Quanta and similar companies is a reminder that even businesses selling the essential tools of a boom can see their stock prices swing widely when expectations run high. The underlying questions are straightforward: how much will the biggest technology companies keep spending, how fast can the physical infrastructure be built, and how much of that outlook is already reflected in prices? Anyone considering investments in this area should do their own research, weigh their own goals and risk tolerance, and consider consulting a licensed financial professional.
